transcript.text: Samsung WD90T534DBW washer dryer - clothes are still damp at the end of the wash and dry programme. It's not that old. Is the heater going?

It could be a heating fault, but on a washer-dryer it is not the most common explanation—especially if it is relatively new.

The WD90T534DBW is a 9 kg washer but only about 6 kg dryer. A very common cause is washing a full 8–9 kg load and then selecting Wash + Dry: it can wash that amount, but cannot dry it properly. The result is warm, damp clothes at the end.

Try this before assuming the heater has failed:

1. Use a small drying load
   Try 2–3 large towels, or roughly half a drum, not packed in. Choose a Cotton dry setting or a timed dry programme.

2. Make sure it spun properly first
   Select a high spin (e.g. 1200–1400 rpm where fabric allows). If clothes are still very wet/heavy rather than merely damp, the issue may be draining or spinning rather than drying.

3. Clean the drain-pump filter
   A partial blockage can prevent a good spin. Switch off/unplug first, put towels and a shallow tray down, then clean the filter behind the lower front flap. Expect some water.

4. Do not judge it too soon
   Washer-dryer drying cycles can take several hours and may adjust their time automatically. “Iron dry” intentionally leaves clothes slightly damp; use “Cupboard dry” or an appropriate timed dry option if you want them fully dry.

5. Check whether it is actually producing heat
   On a small load, after around 20–30 minutes of drying, the drum/clothes should feel noticeably warm (take care—do not force the door or interrupt unnecessarily). If it remains completely cold and the programme runs/finishes normally, a drying-heater, temperature sensor, fan, wiring or control-board issue becomes more likely.

A heater fault is particularly plausible if:

• drying loads stay cold and wet, even when small;
• a timed dry programme does not heat;
• wash programmes that should heat water also seem to wash in cold water;
• it displays an error code or ends unusually quickly.

However, don’t dismantle the machine or test the heater live—there are mains-voltage parts and, depending on the version, drying components that need proper diagnosis.

If the small-load/timed-dry test still leaves items cold and damp, contact Samsung or the retailer for a warranty repair. Have the model and serial number ready, and report: “small load, high-spin beforehand, timed dry selected, no heat / clothes cold and wet at end.”
I usually load the full 9kg drum and do Wash+Dry with Cupboard Dry. The drum does get hot and the clothes are hot but damp at the end. I often turn the spin down to 800 too. No error codes.

That strongly suggests the heater is working. If the drum and clothes are hot, but the load is damp, the main issue is almost certainly too much laundry for the drying capacity, made worse by the reduced spin speed.

Your machine can wash 9 kg, but it can only dry about 6 kg—and in real use, for reliably dry “Cupboard Dry” results, 4–5 kg is often more realistic, especially for towels, jeans, bedding, or thick cottons. A 9 kg wash load fills the drum; when drying, the clothes cannot tumble freely enough for moisture to evaporate and condense away efficiently.

Dropping the spin to 800 rpm also leaves a great deal more water in the load than 1200–1400 rpm. The dryer then has to remove that extra water, often beyond what the combined Wash + Dry programme can manage within its designed time.

What to do:

• For Wash + Dry, load no more than around half to two-thirds of the drum—ideally up to the 6 kg drying rating, less for bulky items.
• Use 1400 rpm for cottons/towels where the care labels permit it. Use 1200 if 1400 is unsuitable.
• If you want to wash a full 9 kg load, run the wash first, then remove roughly a third to half of it before drying in two batches.
• Avoid mixing heavy items (towels, jeans) with light synthetics/shirts where possible; the sensor may finish when lighter items seem dry while heavy items remain damp.
• If the load is merely hot and slightly damp, an extra timed dry cycle on a smaller load may finish it—but it is better to reduce the load from the start.

“Cupboard Dry” is normally intended to leave clothes dry enough to put away, though thick seams, waistbands, towels and pockets can still feel a little damp immediately after the programme. Letting the load sit spread out for 5–10 minutes can sometimes equalise that residual moisture.

A useful test: wash/spin a modest cotton load at 1400 rpm, no more than half a drum, then run Cupboard Dry. If that comes out properly dry, there is no indication of a failed heater or major machine fault.
